problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t),\,y=t-\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)$
from $t=0$ to $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ ?

examples.knowledge_point: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions
examples.problem:
Find the expression that gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t, \, y=\ln{(\cos{t})}$
from $t=0$ to $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (see graph below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/48de26c11ae08afb45ec19ee56e770f7418f9be2afb8ee7dd46a0d1136cb125b.png)
examples.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡t))=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+{tan}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Which of the following gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x={t}^{3}-8,\,y={t}^{4}+5t$
from $t=-2$ to $t=3$ ?
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-8)=3{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}+5t)=4{t}^{3}+5\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{{(3{t}^{2})}^{2}+{(4{t}^{3}+5)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+16{t}^{6}+40{t}^{3}+25}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{3}\sqrt{16{t}^{6}+9{t}^{4}+40{t}^{3}+25}\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$
